## Alternative proofs

### logic:hennessy-milner — Game-theoretic / greatest-fixpoint proof

**Idea.** View bisimilarity as the greatest fixpoint of a monotone operator and use the finite-branching hypothesis to show that the complement of modal equivalence is closed under the operator's one-step removal, i.e. that modal equivalence itself is a post-fixpoint, hence contained in the greatest fixpoint.

1. Step 1 — Short Claim: The operator $\Phi$ sending a relation $S\subset W\times W'$ to the set of pairs $(v,v')$ that agree on propositional variables and satisfy the forth and back conditions with respect to $S$ is monotone, and bisimilarity is its greatest fixpoint $\nu\Phi$ (Kleene: $\nu\Phi=\bigcap_{n}\Phi^{n}(W\times W')$). (Standard fixpoint theory on a finite powerset lattice is not needed; the intersection description holds for any monotone $\Phi$ on a complete lattice by Tarski–Knaster.)
2. Step 2 — Short Claim: $v\mathrel{\underline{\leftrightarrow}}_{n}v'$ iff $(v,v')\in\Phi^{n}(W\times W')$. (Induction on $n$ from the definitions of $n$-bisimulation and of $\Phi$.)
3. Step 3 — Short Claim: If $v,v'$ are modally equivalent then $(v,v')\in\Phi^{n}(W\times W')$ for every $n$, hence $v\mathrel{\underline{\leftrightarrow}}_{n}v'$ for every $n$. (Induction on $n$: the case $n=0$ is agreement on propositional variables; for $n+1$, given $vRu$, if no $R'$-successor of $v'$ were $n$-bisimilar to $u$, the finite set $\{u'_{1},\dots,u'_{k}\}$ of successors of $v'$ would yield, exactly as in the given Step 1, a formula $\Diamond D$ true at $v$ and false at $v'$.)
4. Step 4 — Short Claim: On image-finite models, $\bigcap_{n}\Phi^{n}(W\times W')$ is itself a bisimulation, i.e. $\Phi(\bigcap_{n}\Phi^{n})=\bigcap_{n}\Phi^{n}$. (Forth: if $v$ is $n$-bisimilar to $v'$ for all $n$ and $vRu$, then for each $n$ some successor $u'_{n}$ of $v'$ is $(n-1)$-bisimilar to $u$; by image-finiteness some single $u'$ occurs for infinitely many $n$, hence for all $n$, and $u,u'$ are $n$-bisimilar for all $n$. Back is symmetric.)
5. Step 5 — Short Claim: Modal equivalence implies bisimilarity. (Combine Steps 3 and 4: modal equivalence is contained in $\bigcap_{n}\Phi^{n}$, which is a bisimulation.)

**Prerequisites.** Definition of $n$-bisimulation and the fact that modal equivalence implies $n$-bisimilarity for all $n$ (which is essentially item 3 of \ref{logic:n-bisimulation-basic}, proved by the same finite-conjunction argument); Tarski–Knaster or just the elementary description of $\bigcap_{n}\Phi^{n}(W\times W')$; image-finiteness used only in Step 4 (pigeonhole on an infinite subset of a finite set).

**Why instructive.** It isolates exactly where image-finiteness enters (a pigeonhole argument in Step 4) and exhibits bisimilarity as a coinductive greatest fixpoint, which is the standard formulation in concurrency theory and the one that generalizes to coalgebra and to the infinite-conjunction languages mentioned in the hypcheck.

### logic:finite-tree-model — Selection by maximal consistent Hintikka sets (pruning the unravelling)

**Idea.** Instead of building the tree top-down by choosing witnesses for false boxed formulas, take the unravelling of $\mathcal{M}$ from $w$, and prune it: keep only nodes whose label sequence is 'justified' by a Hintikka-style set of subformulas of degree at most the remaining depth. The bound on branching comes from the number of boxed subformulas, and the bound on depth from $d(A)$.

1. Step 1 — Short Claim: For each node $s$ of the unravelling $\mathcal{M}^{\to}_{w}$ at depth $\ell\le m=d(A)$ one can choose a propositionally consistent set $X_{s}\subset\mathrm{Sub}_{m-\ell}(A)$ with $\mathrm{last}(s)\in$ (the world of $s$) satisfying $B\in X_{s}\iff\mathcal{M},\mathrm{last}(s)\models B$; in particular $A\in X_{(w)}$. (Take $X_{s}$ to be the set of subformulas of degree at most $m-\ell$ true at $\mathrm{last}(s)$; consistency is immediate from the truth definition.)
2. Step 2 — Short Claim: For each node $s$ at depth $\ell<m$ and each $\Box C\in\mathrm{Sub}_{m-\ell}(A)$ with $\Box C\notin X_{s}$, there is a successor $t$ of $s$ in the unravelling with $C\notin X_{t}$. (Since $\mathcal{M},\mathrm{last}(s)\not\models\Box C$, pick $v$ with $\mathrm{last}(s)Rv$, $\mathcal{M},v\not\models C$ and let $t$ be $s$ extended by $v$.)
3. Step 3 — Short Claim: One can choose, for each node $s$ at depth $\ell<m$, a set $Y_{s}$ of at most $k$ successors of $s$ in the unravelling such that every $\Box C\in\mathrm{Sub}_{m-\ell}(A)\setminus X_{s}$ is refuted at some member of $Y_{s}$. (Choose one witness per such $\Box C$ by Step 2; there are at most $k$ of them, and the choices are finite.)
4. Step 4 — Short Claim: The subtree $\mathcal{T}$ of the unravelling consisting of the nodes reachable from $(w)$ through the chosen sets $Y_{s}$ is a finite tree of depth at most $m$ and branching at most $k$, and for every node $s$ of $\mathcal{T}$ at depth $\ell$ and every $B\in\mathrm{Sub}_{m-\ell}(A)$, $\mathcal{T},s\models B\iff\mathcal{M},\mathrm{last}(s)\models B$. (Induction on $B$; the box case uses that all children of $s$ in $\mathcal{T}$ are children in the unravelling, and that a false $\Box C$ has a chosen child refuting $C$.)
5. Step 5 — Short Claim: $\mathcal{T},(w)\models A$. (Step 4 with $s=(w)$, $\ell=0$, $B=A$, using $\mathcal{M},w\models A$.)

**Prerequisites.** The unravelling and \ref{logic:unravelling-bisimilar} (or just the definition of $W^{\to}$ and $\mathrm{last}$); the observation that $\Box D\in\mathrm{Sub}_{m}(A)$ implies $D\in\mathrm{Sub}_{m-1}(A)$; no compactness or choice beyond finitely many selections.

**Why instructive.** It makes clear that the finite tree is a pruned subtree of the unravelling, so the truth-preservation argument is a straightforward induction along the tree rather than a construction that has to be checked for consistency with $\mathcal{M}$ at every step; it also shows the two bounds (depth $d(A)$, branching = number of boxed subformulas) come from two different constraints.

### logic:k-pspace — Alternating / game view of the Hintikka recursion (Savitch-free space analysis)

**Idea.** Present the decision procedure as a two-player game between the algorithm (choosing the set $X$) and an adversary (choosing the false boxed formula), and analyse space by the same recursion but with an explicit bound on the number of simultaneously stored sets, making the polynomial-space claim transparent.

1. Step 1 — Short Claim: $\mathrm{Sat}(T,F,m)$ holds iff the adversary-player has no winning strategy in the following game: the algorithm picks a propositionally consistent $X\supset T$ with $X\cap F=\varnothing$; the adversary picks $\Box C\in\mathrm{Sub}_{m}(A)\setminus X$; the play continues with $\mathrm{Sat}(\{D:\Box D\in X\},\{C\},m-1)$; the algorithm wins if the adversary cannot move. (Immediate reformulation of \ref{logic:k-satisfiability-recursion}.)
2. Step 2 — Short Claim: The game tree has depth at most $d(A)+1$ and each position is described by $O(n)$ bits ($T$, $F$, $m$ and the current $\Box C$). (Counting: subsets of $\mathrm{Sub}(A)$ are $n$-bit strings, $m\le n$.)
3. Step 3 — Short Claim: A depth-first evaluation of the game tree, storing one position per level, uses $O(n^{2})$ space and decides $\mathrm{Sat}(\{A\},\varnothing,d(A))$. (Standard depth-first search on a tree of depth $\le n$ with $O(n)$-bit positions; the branching is exponential but time is unconstrained.)
4. Step 4 — Short Claim: $\mathsf{K}$-satisfiability is in PSPACE, and so is $\mathsf{K}$-provability. (Step 3 plus soundness and completeness of $\mathsf{K}$ and closure of PSPACE under complement.)

**Prerequisites.** \ref{logic:k-satisfiability-recursion}; basic facts about PSPACE (\ref{comp:class-pspace}); no Savitch theorem needed since the procedure is deterministic.

**Why instructive.** It separates the two resources cleanly: the exponential blow-up is in the branching (time), while the depth of the recursion is what controls space. This is the standard intuition behind PSPACE algorithms for modal and temporal logics and explains why the depth bound $d(A)$ in the characterization is essential.

## Alternative definitions

### logic:bisimulation (equivalent)

A bisimulation between $\mathcal{M}=(W,R,V)$ and $\mathcal{M}'=(W',R',V')$ is a relation $Z\subset W\times W'$ such that for all $wZw'$: (i) $w$ and $w'$ satisfy the same propositional variables; (ii) for every $v$ with $wRv$ there is $v'$ with $w'R'v'$ and $vZv'$; (iii) for every $v'$ with $w'R'v'$ there is $v$ with $wRv$ and $vZv'$. Equivalently: $Z$ is a bisimulation iff $Z\subset\Phi(Z)$, where $\Phi$ is the monotone operator of the alternative proof above; and $\mathrel{\underline{\leftrightarrow}}$ is the greatest fixpoint $\nu\Phi$, i.e. the union of all bisimulations.

**Conditions.** Same setting (any Kripke models, no finiteness assumptions).

**Equivalence.** The two formulations are literally the same clauses; the fixpoint formulation only repackages them. The union of bisimulations is again a bisimulation (each clause is preserved by unions), so a greatest bisimulation exists and coincides with $\nu\Phi$ by Tarski–Knaster; $w\mathrel{\underline{\leftrightarrow}}w'$ iff $(w,w')\in\nu\Phi$.

**Reference.** Blackburn, de Rijke, Venema, Modal Logic, Chapter 2 (bisimulations and the greatest bisimulation); Sangiorgi, Introduction to Bisimulation and Coinduction.

### logic:bisimulation (equivalent)

A bisimulation is a relation $Z$ such that $Z\subset\Phi(Z)$ where $\Phi(Z)$ consists of the pairs agreeing on propositional variables and satisfying the forth and back conditions with respect to $Z$; bisimilarity is $\nu\Phi=\bigcup\{Z:Z\subset\Phi(Z)\}$.

**Conditions.** Any models; note that this is the same as the previous item, recorded separately because the fixpoint phrasing is the one used in coalgebra and in process algebra.

**Equivalence.** See previous item.

**Reference.** Rutten, 'Universal coalgebra: a theory of systems', Theoretical Computer Science 249 (2000).

### logic:bounded-morphism (equivalent)

A bounded morphism (p-morphism) from $\mathcal{M}$ to $\mathcal{M}'$ is a function $f\colon W\to W'$ whose graph $\{(w,f(w)):w\in W\}$ is a bisimulation; equivalently, $f$ preserves propositional variables, is a homomorphism for $R$ (forth), and satisfies the back condition.

**Conditions.** Same models; the graph formulation is equivalent to the three numbered clauses of the definition.

**Equivalence.** The graph of $f$ satisfies the atomic clause iff $f$ preserves propositional variables; the forth condition for the graph is exactly $wRv\Rightarrow f(w)R'f(v)$; the back condition for the graph is exactly the clause that every $R'$-successor of $f(w)$ is the image of an $R$-successor of $w$. Hence the two definitions coincide.

**Reference.** Blackburn, de Rijke, Venema, Modal Logic, Section 2.1 (bounded morphisms, also called p-morphisms).

### logic:image-finite (NOT equivalent)

A model is image-finite if for every $w$ the set $R[w]$ of successors is finite. A weaker standard variant: a model is finitely branching if each $R[w]$ is finite (same notion), and a genuinely different variant is 'image-countable' or 'locally finite' where only $R[w]$ is required to be finite for the points of interest; the Hennessy–Milner theorem fails for image-countable models (see \ref{logic:hm-counterexample}).

**Conditions.** Image-finiteness is exactly finite branching; the variant 'every $R[w]$ is at most countable' is strictly weaker and does NOT support \ref{logic:hennessy-milner}.

**Equivalence.** The counterexample \ref{logic:hm-counterexample} has a root with countably many successors and shows modal equivalence without bisimilarity, so the countably-branching variant is not equivalent for the purpose of the theorem.

**Reference.** Hennessy and Milner, 'Algebraic laws for nondeterminism and concurrency', J. ACM 32 (1985).

### logic:filtration (equivalent)

A filtration of $\mathcal{M}$ through a finite subformula-closed $\Sigma$ is any model $\mathcal{M}^{f}$ on the set of $\equiv_{\Sigma}$-classes such that (1) $[w]$ satisfies exactly the propositional variables in $\Sigma$ that $w$ satisfies, (2) $wRv$ implies $[w]R^{f}[v]$, and (3) $[w]R^{f}[v]$ implies that for every $\Box B\in\Sigma$, $\mathcal{M},w\models\Box B$ entails $\mathcal{M},v\models B$. Equivalently (standard variant): $\mathcal{M}^{f}$ is a model on $W^{f}$ such that for all $w$, $\mathcal{M},w$ and $\mathcal{M}^{f},[w]$ satisfy the same formulas of $\Sigma$ and $R^{f}$ satisfies (2) and (3).

**Conditions.** $\Sigma$ finite and closed under subformulas; the second phrasing is equivalent because (1)–(3) imply the truth-preservation lemma and, conversely, truth preservation for all $B\in\Sigma$ forces (1) and (3) (take $B$ a propositional variable, resp. use $\Box B$).

**Equivalence.** Given (1)–(3), the filtration lemma gives truth preservation by induction. Conversely, if $\mathcal{M}^{f}$ preserves all formulas of $\Sigma$ at every $[w]$, then (1) holds for propositional variables in $\Sigma$, and (3) holds because $\mathcal{M},w\models\Box B$ with $\Box B\in\Sigma$ gives $\mathcal{M}^{f},[w]\models\Box B$, which together with $[w]R^{f}[v]$ gives $\mathcal{M}^{f},[v]\models B$ and hence $\mathcal{M},v\models B$.

**Reference.** Blackburn, de Rijke, Venema, Modal Logic, Section 2.3 (filtration); Chagrov and Zakharyaschev, Modal Logic, Chapter 5.

### logic:modal-satisfiable (equivalent)

For a normal modal logic $L$ with a class of frames $\mathsf{Fr}(L)$, $A$ is $L$-satisfiable iff $L\nvdash\neg A$; equivalently, iff $A$ is satisfiable in some model based on a frame in $\mathsf{Fr}(L)$.

**Conditions.** Requires soundness and completeness of $L$ with respect to its class of frames (\ref{logic:page-modal-completeness}); without completeness only the implication '$L$-satisfiable $\Rightarrow$ $L\nvdash\neg A$' (soundness) holds.

**Equivalence.** If $A$ is satisfiable at $w$ in a model on an $L$-frame, then $\neg A$ fails at $w$, so $\neg A$ is not valid on $\mathsf{Fr}(L)$, so by soundness $L\nvdash\neg A$. Conversely if $L\nvdash\neg A$, completeness gives a model on an $L$-frame and a world falsifying $\neg A$, i.e. satisfying $A$.

**Reference.** Blackburn, de Rijke, Venema, Modal Logic, Section 1.6 and Chapter 4 (soundness, completeness and satisfiability).
